title: Sain hyvää palvelua Espoon autohuollossa
subtitle: I got good service at the Espoo car service centre

blocks.text: Back in Lesson 2, you saw autohuoltoon — 'to the car service centre' — without stopping to explain it. Finnish doesn't use prepositions like English 'in', 'to', 'from' — it changes the ending of the noun itself instead. This lesson gives you the three endings that do that job for places: being in one, going into one, and coming from one.

blocks.annotated: Sain hyvää palvelua Espoon {autohuollossa|grammar|inessive|at the car service centre}.
blocks.translation: I got good service at the Espoo car service centre.

blocks.title: No prepositions, just endings
blocks.text: English needs three separate little words — in, to, from — to do what Finnish does by changing the tail of one word: autohuolto, autohuollossa, autohuoltoon, autohuollosta. Reviewers name the shop constantly, so these place-endings appear on almost every business name in the corpus.

blocks.content: To say something is inside or at a place, add {-ssa|grammar|inessive suffix|in/at} after back vowels (a, o, u) or {-ssä|grammar|inessive suffix|in/at} after front vowels (ä, ö, y) — the same vowel harmony rule from Lesson 2's -sta/-stä. Autohuolto → autohuollossa, 'at the car service centre'.

items.fi: Sain palvelua Espoon {autohuollossa|grammar|inessive|at the car service centre}.
items.en: I got service at the Espoo car service centre.

items.fi: Hinta oli kohtuullinen tässä {korjaamossa|grammar|inessive|at this repair shop}.
items.en: The price was reasonable at this repair shop.

blocks.text: Piece 2 — Illative: going into a place

blocks.content: You met this one already in Lesson 2: autohuoltoon, 'into/to the car service centre'. This is the {illative|grammar|case name|into} case. Its ending varies more than -ssa does — often -Vn (doubling the last vowel + n), sometimes -hVn or -seen for longer words — but the meaning is always 'movement into'.

items.fi: Vein autoni Espoon {autohuoltoon|grammar|illative|into the car service centre}.
items.en: I took my car to the Espoo car service centre.
I took the car in for service.
It went into the repair shop.

blocks.title: Elative — the third leg of the triangle
blocks.text: The elative case, {-sta|grammar|elative suffix|from} or {-stä|grammar|elative suffix|from}, marks 'out of/from'. Same vowel harmony rule as always: back vowels get -sta, front vowels get -stä. Now you have all three: autohuollossa (at), autohuoltoon (into), autohuollosta (from) — one noun, three endings, three directions.

items.fi: Korjautin autoni muualla, ei tästä {korjaamosta|grammar|elative|from this repair shop}.
items.en: I got my car fixed elsewhere, not from this repair shop.
I called back from the repair shop.
The fault was found during the service.

lines.speaker: B
lines.fi: Sain palvelua Espoon autohuollossa. Vein autoni sinne autohuoltoon eilen.
lines.en: I got service at the Espoo car service centre. I took my car there yesterday.

lines.speaker: A
lines.en: Where did you hear about the place from?

lines.speaker: B
lines.en: I heard about that repair shop from a friend.

blocks.title: Paul Noble Rule
blocks.text: Don't memorise these three endings as separate words. Picture one triangle: -ssa (staying in), -Vn (going into), -sta (coming from). Every place name in Finnish — a shop, a city, a room — cycles through this exact same triangle. Learn the shape once, apply it everywhere.

blocks.content: Autohuollossa: AU-to-huol-los-sa (long word — the double 's' and double 'o' both get held slightly). Autohuoltoon: AU-to-huol-toon (long final 'oo', that's the illative marker doing its job). Korjaamosta: KOR-yaa-mos-ta (the double 'aa' stays long even with the ending attached).

blocks.title: What you now own
items: how one noun like autohuolto cycles through all three: autohuollossa, autohuoltoon, autohuollosta
you can now say where you got service, where you took the car, and where a fault was found
you can apply this same triangle to any new place name you meet later, without needing a new rule
